name: Wei Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I help build the timber stairs at the Ferry Quay apartments. I'm fifty-eight and the junior on the crew after years working in a furniture warehouse; I left school early and still need the lead joiner to check my more difficult cuts. My partner Mara teaches music lessons, and our grown daughter works in another town. This site pays well and we have eleven months of expenses saved. I use an AI assistant every day to turn rough stair notes into a cutting list, then put a square against the timber before any saw starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the assistant already saves me time finding a drawing note, so a modest improvement would be welcome. I would keep the final checks with the person holding the timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income seems safe in this picture; the Ferry Quay job has months to run and there are many builders in town. Mara's lessons fluctuate, but our eleven-month reserve means a slow term will not send us scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on with the stairs and use my assistant to sort the daily list. During the first year I'd keep our usual savings deposit and show lead joiner Pavel any AI answer that changes a dimension before I cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable with the tool and the work ahead. I am still learning the trade, so a good list is useful precisely because I know it can be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was the list wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week it treated a landing measurement as a tread length, and Pavel spotted the mismatch on the drawing. We corrected the page before the saw touched a board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you automate the cutting itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't own the site's machines and wouldn't change them on a phone suggestion. The square and the drawing still get the last word on a cut.

say: I'd welcome **faster drawing notes** while leaving final checks with the worker.
I'd tell the crew an **AI list** still needs a square and drawing.
think: My **site income** looks secure while Ferry Quay has work booked.
Our **eleven-month reserve** covers Mara's uneven lesson weeks.
do: Keep building **timber stairs** and using the daily AI list.
Show Pavel any **changed dimension** before cutting timber.
feel: **Comfortable** with modest change and careful about junior mistakes.
S0.quote: The square and the drawing still get the last word on a cut.
fieldNote: Wei's daily AI use has a **recent measurement error** attached to it, which keeps checking central.
A booked project, higher pay and an **eleven-month reserve** support his calm response.

steps.text: Keep building stairs at the Ferry Quay apartments
Use the AI cutting list with drawing and square checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning software could cut wasted trips for the crew if its dates and quantities are right. I'd offer to test the ordering screen on one stair flight and show everyone what went wrong as well as what worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the office doing more with fewer people, and a badly handled change could leave us without the next contract. My own hands still build stairs, but as a late-entry junior I cannot treat the site roster as guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Pavel to let me compare one AI material order with the crate that arrives. In the first year I'll keep taking paid shifts and add the order results to my work notebook; if the next job slips a month, I'll send applications to two local joinery crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the experiment and uneasy about the contract book. Mara's lesson income is too uneven to make my wage optional, even with savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order date, the lengths requested, the actual crate and any hours spent putting it right. A green tick on a screen does not tell us whether the timber reached the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a month before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A week's delay is common on building sites, and the reserve covers that easily. A month without a new start would be a sign I should look while I'm still employed.

say: I'd offer a **one-flight order trial** and share both mistakes and gains.
I'd judge software by **delivered timber**, not screen ticks.
think: Fewer office staff could leave the crew waiting for **new contracts**.
My **junior place** and Mara's uneven lessons make the roster important.
do: Compare an **AI material order** with its delivered crate.
Keep **paid shifts** and record corrections in my notebook.
Apply to **local joinery crews** after a month-long project slip.
feel: **Interested and uneasy** while the next contract remains uncertain.
S1.quote: A green tick on a screen does not tell us whether the timber reached the stairs.
fieldNote: Wei volunteers a **measured order trial**, including the hours needed to correct an error.
His month-long trigger for applications distinguishes normal site delay from an **income threat**.

steps.text: Trial the AI ordering screen on a stair-flight material order
Keep taking paid Ferry Quay shifts
Apply to two joinery crews if the next job slips a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the 2028 thinking system might design the stairs before a person measures them, but the crew still has boards to fit until robots arrive around 2031. I want the firm to test any site robot in plain view, not behind a sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when drawings can be made by cheaper AI and sixty-three when robots could cut and fit stairs. Our savings can cover a search, but losing my higher site wage for years would change the retirement Mara and I are trying to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll test the digital stair checker with Pavel and put extra away after full paid months. In 2029 I'll keep taking stair shifts, then apply to local repair teams if the roster thins; I'd ask for their actual rates before I leave this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a substantial wage once hands-on robots arrive. I can use the time, but a screen skill alone will not protect my fitting hours after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the checker have to catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should spot a tread count that fails the building drawing and flag it before we order timber. Pavel and I would run it alongside our normal check on a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot for side work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put eleven months of living money into a machine whose repairs and customers I cannot predict. I'd rather apply for a wage-paying repair job than gamble the household reserve.

say: I'd separate **2028 stair design** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd demand a **visible site trial** before working with robots.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my paid stair fitting.
Our **reserve** covers a search but not years without my higher wage.
do: Test the **stair checker** with Pavel and save extra.
Keep **paid stair shifts** in 2029 while offered.
Apply to **repair teams** if the roster thins.
feel: **Anxious** about losing fitting income despite a usable search cushion.
S2.quote: I can use the time, but a screen skill alone will not protect my fitting hours after 2031.
fieldNote: Wei does not mistake his **daily AI skill** for protection against later hands-on automation.
His refusal to buy a robot protects the **household reserve** despite his willingness to test site tools.

steps.text: Test the digital stair checker with Pavel on a paid job
Save extra after full paid months
Keep taking paid stair shifts in 2029
Apply to local repair teams if site shifts thin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years is long enough to learn which digital checks help and to ask the builder for a clear equipment plan. I would keep a record of what our crew can do, not just what a demonstration claims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three, thinking AI may change the design work and the flow of jobs; at sixty-six, robots might fit the stairs. Mara and I may have enough saved to ease off by then, but a retirement date needs our actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep testing useful drawing checks and take photos of completed stair flights, with Pavel's sign-off where possible. In 2032 I'd keep paid site shifts, ask nearby repair firms about real openings and review our savings with Mara before deciding whether I can reduce work in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more curious than pressed in this version. The extra years give me room to build a record and learn where paid work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a repair firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show stair photos, the job dates and the corrections I made after Pavel checked my work. I am a junior carpenter, so I need evidence beyond saying I worked here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on robot maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a local paid course led to an actual maintenance opening, I'd enrol. I wouldn't sign up just because somebody says robots are the future.

say: I'd ask for an **equipment plan** and records from real crew work.
I'd use five years to test **useful digital checks**.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots may reach my stair fitting.
I can reduce work only after Mara and I check **retirement figures**.
do: Use **drawing checks** and keep paid site shifts in 2032.
Ask **repair firms** about openings before deciding on fewer hours.
feel: More **curious than pressed**, with time to build proof of work.
S3.quote: I am a junior carpenter, so I need evidence beyond saying I worked here.
fieldNote: The longer lead time becomes a **portfolio of stair work** and conditional job enquiries.
His interest in robot maintenance training depends on a **paid course** with an actual opening.

steps.text: Keep a signed photo record of completed stair flights
Use drawing checks on paid stair jobs in 2032
Ask local repair firms about real openings
Enrol in robot maintenance training only if a paid course leads to a local opening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade leaves plenty of time to keep working and see which site tools earn their place. I would tell younger carpenters to learn the drawings as well as the software that reads them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I may still want paid light repair work then, because Mara's lessons and whatever we have saved by that date cannot be known exactly now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep building stairs while fit, use checked AI lists on current jobs and save extra from good months. In 2037 I'd take paid repair calls if needed and sit with Mara to compare our actual income with bills before ending my site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the distant technology, and pleased that there is room to change course if a useful tool appears. My back and the present work schedule deserve attention well before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown daughter for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own life and wages, and Mara and I want to meet our costs ourselves. We might talk through the numbers together, but I would not count her income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could cause an earlier shift to repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my back made full stair flights too hard, I would apply for paid small repairs while there are local openings. A lighter job would still have to pay something we can use.

say: I'd keep **drawing skills** alongside the software that reads plans.
I'd use the **decade** to judge tools on actual site work.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid light repairs may still be needed.
At **seventy-one**, Mara's lesson income and savings decide whether I stop.
do: Keep **stair work** and checked AI lists while fit.
Save extra from **good months** and take paid repairs in 2037 if needed.
Compare **income and bills** with Mara before leaving work.
feel: **Calm and curious** about distant tools, attentive to current health and jobs.
S4.quote: A lighter job would still have to pay something we can use.
fieldNote: Wei combines a **long planning window** with continued paid work and savings, rather than assuming retirement.
He would shift to **small repairs** if his back required it and keeps his daughter's income outside the budget.

steps.text: Keep taking paid stair work while physically able
Use checked AI cutting lists on current jobs
Save extra after strong paid months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because hands-on robots could reach stair work by sixty-three, before our retirement numbers are clear. A visible trial, honest rota dates and paid repair openings would help me use my savings without burning through them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns a wrong drawing after an AI system creates it. The worker cutting the timber needs a way to flag the error before anyone builds it into a stair.

headlineQuote: The worker cutting the timber needs a way to flag the error before anyone builds it into a stair.
portrait: Wei is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter who came from furniture warehousing.
He uses **AI every day**, checking stair lists against drawings and a square.
Higher site pay and an **eleven-month reserve** help cover Mara's uneven music-lesson income.
He seeks **real paid openings** and keeps retirement tied to household figures.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could replace his stair fitting around 2031, before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **visible robot trial**, reliable rota dates and paid repair vacancies.
